question: A tenant restaurant owner installs a large walk-in cooler that is bolted to the floor for use in her business. Under the law of fixtures, this item is best classified as a:
choice_a: Trade fixture, which the tenant may remove before the lease ends as long as she repairs any damage
choice_b: Real property fixture that automatically transfers to the landlord regardless of the lease terms
choice_c: Emblement that must be harvested before the lease terminates
choice_d: License that expires automatically when the tenancy ends
explanation: Trade fixtures are items a business tenant installs to conduct its trade; even though attached, they remain the tenant's personal property and may be removed before the lease expires, provided the tenant repairs any resulting damage to the premises.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A farmer leases land and plants a crop of wheat during the growing season. The lease expires before the wheat is harvested. Under the doctrine of emblements, the crop is treated as:
choice_a: Real property that transfers automatically to the landlord at the end of the lease
choice_b: Personal property (a chattel) that the tenant farmer is entitled to harvest even after the lease ends
choice_c: A fixture that must remain attached to the land permanently
choice_d: Common property owned jointly by landlord and tenant
explanation: Emblements are annual, cultivated crops produced by a tenant's labor. They are treated as personal property, and the doctrine allows the tenant farmer the right to re-enter and harvest the crop even after the tenancy has ended.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A seller removes an ordinary above-ground dishwasher that simply plugs into an outlet and is not built into the cabinetry, taking it with her when she moves. A buyer objects that it should have stayed. Under general fixture law, who is correct?
choice_a: The buyer, because all kitchen appliances are legally fixtures regardless of attachment
choice_b: The seller, because anything purchased more than five years ago is automatically personal property
choice_c: The seller, because a freestanding appliance that is not physically attached to the structure is presumed to be personal property
choice_d: The buyer, because the item was listed in the multiple listing service description of the kitchen
explanation: Method of attachment is a core fixture test. An appliance that is merely plugged in and not bolted, wired in, or built into the structure is ordinarily personal property, so the seller may remove it unless the contract specifically includes it.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: An appraiser is asked to determine whether a custom greenhouse attached to a home passed with the sale. Which of the following fixture tests asks whether removing the item would cause significant damage to the real property?
choice_a: The adaptability of the item to the property's use
choice_b: The intention of the party who installed the item
choice_c: The relationship between the parties to the transaction
choice_d: The method and permanence of attachment
explanation: The method-and-permanence-of-attachment test looks at how firmly and permanently an item is affixed, including whether removal would cause substantial damage to the structure -- a strong indicator the item has become a fixture.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A legal description begins 'Beginning at the iron pipe at the northeast corner of Lot 4, thence South 200 feet, thence West 150 feet, thence North 200 feet, thence East 150 feet to the point of beginning.' This is an example of a:
explanation: Metes and bounds descriptions identify a parcel using a point of beginning, then a series of courses (directions) and distances that trace the boundary back to that same starting point, which is exactly the pattern shown here.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A deed describes property as 'Lot 12, Block 3, Meadowbrook Estates, as recorded in Plat Book 22, Page 14, of the county land records.' This method of legal description relies primarily on:
choice_a: A system of principal meridians and base lines dividing land into 6-mile-square townships
choice_b: A recorded subdivision plat map that has already been surveyed and filed with the county
choice_c: A point of beginning followed by compass directions and distances
choice_d: The property's assessed value for tax purposes
explanation: Lot and block descriptions reference a specific lot and block number shown on a recorded subdivision plat map, which itself contains the detailed metes-and-bounds or survey data for the entire subdivision.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: Under the government (rectangular) survey system, a township is a square area measuring:
explanation: In the government survey system, a township is a 6-mile-by-6-mile square (36 square miles), which is subdivided into 36 sections, each one mile square.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: Under the government (rectangular) survey system, one full section of land contains how many acres?
explanation: A section is one square mile, and one square mile equals 640 acres. Sections are commonly divided further into halves, quarters, and quarter-quarters for smaller parcels.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: When an appraiser calculates a single-family home's gross living area (GLA), which of the following is typically EXCLUDED?
choice_a: An unfinished basement and an attached garage
choice_c: A finished, heated first-floor family room
choice_d: A finished, heated sunroom that is part of the main structure and heated by the same system
explanation: Gross living area generally includes only finished, heated, above-grade living space. Unfinished basements and garages, even if attached, are excluded from GLA and reported separately.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: In commercial office leasing, the difference between rentable square footage and usable square footage is generally accounted for by:
choice_a: The square footage of the tenant's private storage unit in the basement
choice_b: A load factor (or common area factor) representing the tenant's proportionate share of shared spaces such as lobbies, hallways, and restrooms
choice_c: The total square footage of the entire building regardless of tenant
choice_d: The parking area assigned exclusively to that tenant
explanation: Usable square footage is the space a tenant physically occupies; rentable square footage adds a load factor reflecting the tenant's pro-rata share of common areas like lobbies and corridors, and rent is typically charged on the rentable figure.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A rectangular showroom measures 40 feet by 60 feet. What is its total square footage?
explanation: Area of a rectangle equals length multiplied by width: 40 feet x 60 feet = 2,400 square feet.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A parcel of land measures 435.6 feet by 1,000 feet. Approximately how many acres is this?
explanation: One acre equals 43,560 square feet. The parcel's area is 435.6 x 1,000 = 435,600 square feet, and 435,600 divided by 43,560 equals 10 acres.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A property borders a slow-moving, non-navigable river. The water rights that attach to this property because of its location along the river are known as:
explanation: Riparian rights belong to owners of land bordering flowing waters such as rivers and streams. On non-navigable waterways, the riparian owner's title typically extends to the center (thread) of the waterway.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A property is located on the shore of a large lake. The rights this owner holds regarding the lake's water and shoreline are known as:
explanation: Littoral rights apply to property bordering large, substantially non-flowing bodies of water such as lakes, seas, and oceans. Littoral owners generally hold title to the mean high-water mark, with the land below belonging to the public or the state.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: In several western states, water rights in rivers and streams are allocated not based on adjacent land ownership but on which of the following doctrines?
choice_a: Riparian doctrine, under which only adjacent landowners may use the water at all
choice_b: Littoral doctrine, which governs only ocean and lake frontage
choice_c: Prior appropriation, under which the first person to put the water to beneficial use has the superior right
choice_d: Escheat doctrine, under which unclaimed water rights revert to the state
explanation: The prior appropriation doctrine, used in many western states, grants water rights based on who first put the water to beneficial use and when, regardless of whether that user's land actually touches the water source.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A landowner sells the coal and natural gas beneath her property to a mining company while retaining ownership of the surface. This is an example of:
choice_a: An easement in gross benefiting the mining company
choice_b: A license that automatically expires after one year
choice_c: Escheat of the mineral estate to the state
choice_d: Severance of mineral rights from surface rights, creating a subsurface estate separate from the surface estate
explanation: Mineral rights can be severed (separated) from surface rights and conveyed independently, creating two distinct estates in the same land -- a subsurface mineral estate and a surface estate -- that can be owned by different parties.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A developer purchases the right to construct a building in the empty space above an existing rail terminal without owning the land or the terminal itself. What has the developer acquired?
choice_c: A leasehold estate in the terminal
explanation: Air rights are the rights to use, control, or occupy the vertical space above a parcel of land. They can be sold or leased separately from the surface, commonly seen with construction over rail yards or highways in dense urban areas.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A bank records a mortgage against a homeowner's property to secure repayment of a loan. This mortgage is best classified as what type of encumbrance?
choice_b: A financial lien against the property
explanation: A lien is a financial encumbrance that gives a creditor a claim against property as security for a debt. A mortgage is a voluntary lien the owner places on the property to secure the loan used to purchase or refinance it.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: Parcel A has no direct access to a public road except by crossing Parcel B. A recorded easement allows the owner of Parcel A to cross Parcel B for ingress and egress, and this right transfers automatically to future owners of Parcel A. This is an example of:
choice_a: An easement in gross, personal to the current owner of Parcel A only
choice_b: A license, which is revocable at any time
choice_c: An easement appurtenant, with Parcel A as the dominant estate and Parcel B as the servient estate
explanation: An easement appurtenant benefits one parcel (the dominant estate) and burdens another (the servient estate), and it runs with the land, automatically passing to successive owners of both parcels.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A utility company holds a recorded right to maintain power lines across a homeowner's land, but this right is not tied to ownership of any neighboring parcel and belongs to the utility company itself. This is an example of:
explanation: An easement in gross benefits a specific person or company rather than a neighboring parcel of land. Utility easements are the classic example, since there is no dominant estate -- only a servient estate burdened for the utility's benefit.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A homeowner gives a neighbor verbal permission to walk across her backyard as a shortcut to the lake. The homeowner can revoke this permission at any time. This arrangement is best described as a:
explanation: A license is a personal, revocable, and non-assignable permission to use another's land for a specific purpose. Unlike an easement, it does not run with the land and can be withdrawn by the landowner at will.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A survey reveals that a neighbor's fence extends 3 feet onto the subject property along the shared boundary line. This physical intrusion is called an:
explanation: An encroachment occurs when a structure or improvement, such as a fence, wall, or roof overhang, unlawfully extends onto an adjoining owner's property, typically discovered through a boundary survey.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: Three unrelated investors purchase an office building together. Their deed grants them unequal ownership percentages (50%, 30%, and 20%), and each may sell, transfer, or will his or her share independently without the consent of the others. Upon the death of one investor, that share passes to his heirs rather than to the surviving co-owners. This is a:
choice_a: Joint tenancy with right of survivorship
explanation: Tenancy in common allows co-owners to hold unequal, undivided interests, each freely transferable and inheritable, with no right of survivorship -- exactly the arrangement described.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: Two unrelated business partners take title to a warehouse as joint tenants with right of survivorship. When one partner dies, what happens to that partner's ownership interest?
choice_a: It passes to the deceased partner's heirs according to the will
choice_c: It is divided equally between the surviving joint tenant and the deceased partner's estate
choice_d: It passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant, regardless of what the deceased partner's will states
explanation: The defining feature of joint tenancy with right of survivorship is that a deceased joint tenant's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s) by operation of law, bypassing probate and overriding any conflicting will provision.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A married couple takes title to their home in a form of ownership available only to married persons, which includes a right of survivorship and protects the property from the individual debts of only one spouse. This is:
explanation: Tenancy by the entirety is reserved for married couples, includes an automatic right of survivorship, and generally shields the property from a judgment against only one spouse individually, since neither spouse can convey or encumber the whole without the other's consent.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A grantor conveys property 'to my nephew for the life of my sister,' with the remainder to a charity. The nephew's interest is best described as a:
choice_b: Life estate pur autre vie, measured by the life of a person other than the life tenant himself
explanation: A life estate pur autre vie is measured by the life of someone other than the life tenant -- here, the nephew holds the estate only for as long as his sister remains alive, after which the property passes to the named remainderman (the charity).
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A grantor conveys a life estate to her elderly aunt, with the deed stating that upon the aunt's death, title will revert back to the grantor. The grantor's future interest in this scenario is called a:
explanation: When the future interest following a life estate goes back to the original grantor (or the grantor's heirs) rather than to a third party, it is called a reversion. If it instead passes to a named third party, it is called a remainder.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A buyer purchases a residential condominium unit. In addition to fee simple ownership of the interior airspace of the unit, what interest does the buyer typically also acquire?
choice_a: Shares in a corporation that owns the entire building
choice_b: A proprietary lease to occupy the unit
choice_c: A leasehold interest in the unit only, with no ownership interest at all
choice_d: An undivided tenancy-in-common interest in the building's common elements, such as the lobby, roof, and grounds
explanation: Condominium ownership combines fee simple title to the individual unit with an undivided tenancy-in-common interest, shared with all other unit owners, in the building's common elements and land.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A buyer purchases an apartment in a building where he receives shares of stock in the corporation that owns the entire building, along with a proprietary lease giving him the right to occupy a specific unit. This describes:
explanation: In a cooperative, a corporation holds title to the entire building, and residents own shares of the corporation rather than real property directly, with a proprietary lease granting the right to occupy a specific unit.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A buyer purchases the right to use a beachfront condo unit for one specific week every year, without owning the unit outright for the rest of the year. This is best described as:
choice_b: A timeshare (interval ownership or right-to-use arrangement)
choice_d: A leasehold estate for a term of one year
explanation: A timeshare divides the use of a property into fixed time intervals among multiple owners or users. It can be structured as fee interval ownership (a deeded fractional fee interest) or as a right-to-use arrangement (a contractual, non-ownership license for recurring use).
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: An individual buys a vacation home and takes title in her name alone, with no co-owners of any kind. This form of ownership is known as:
explanation: Ownership in severalty means title is held by a single person or single legal entity, with no co-owners -- the term comes from the owner's interest being 'severed' or separate from any other party.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A property owner transfers legal title to a piece of real estate to a trustee, who manages the property for the benefit of a named beneficiary who holds equitable title. This arrangement is known as:
choice_d: A trust, in which the trustee holds legal title while the beneficiary holds equitable (beneficial) title
explanation: In a real estate trust, the grantor (settlor) conveys legal title to a trustee, who has a fiduciary duty to manage the property for the benefit of the beneficiary, who holds equitable title and the beneficial enjoyment of the property.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (broker-level: property held in trust)

question: A real estate investor uses a land trust to take title to an investment property, naming herself as beneficiary but appointing a trustee to hold recorded legal title. From a brokerage standpoint, one common reason investors use this structure is to:
choice_a: Keep the beneficial owner's identity out of the public land records, since the trustee's name appears on the recorded deed
choice_b: Avoid ever paying property taxes on the parcel
choice_c: Automatically convert the property into a condominium form of ownership
choice_d: Eliminate the need for title insurance at closing
explanation: A land trust allows a trustee to hold recorded legal title while the actual beneficiary's identity remains private, since only the trustee's name appears in the public record; brokers handling trust-held property must still verify who holds authority to sign on the trust's behalf.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (broker-level: property held in trust)
